# Posterior Refinement: Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps

Jaehoon Yoo

###### Abstract

Non-autoregressive generation offers a powerful paradigm for iterative
refinement, allowing models to recursively critique, erase and
regenerate arbitrary subsets of tokens. However, existing
non-autoregressive models fail to realize this potential. Masked
Diffusion Models (MDMs) suffer from factorization error, causing sample
quality to collapse when generating multiple tokens simultaneously. Flow
Map Language Models (FMLMs) circumvent this bottleneck via joint
sequence transport for excellent few-step generation, but sacrifice the
inference-time flexibility of MDMs. We introduce $`\text{FMLM}+`$, a
framework that bridges this gap by equipping FMLM with masking-style
noise schedules. While generating the full sequence in a single step,
$`\text{FMLM}+`$ simultaneously scores the global consistency of each
token _a posteriori_. We leverage this to introduce _Posterior
Refinement_, a novel inference-time refinement strategy that enables the
model to adaptively self-correct its outputs, matching the performance
of discrete baselines with $`32\times`$ fewer NFEs. Across diverse
benchmarks, we demonstrate that $`\text{FMLM}+`$ with Posterior
Refinement improves the speed–quality tradeoff over both MDM and FMLM
families, providing a scalable foundation for high-fidelity language
modeling.

## Introduction

Figure 1: Iterative refinement. $`\text{FMLM}+`$ _unlocks_
self-correction capabilities, outperforming all diffusion baselines with
1024 function evaluations using as few as $`32`$ rounds of Posterior
Refinement.

Contemporary language models are predominantly autoregressive (AR),
necessitating $`L`$ sequential forward passes to generate a sequence of
length $`L`$ \[[1](#bib.bib26), [2](#bib.bib25), [3](#bib.bib27)\].
While this paradigm has scaled remarkably well, its inherent sequential
bottleneck makes inference slow and memory-bound \[[4](#bib.bib11),
[5](#bib.bib57)\]. These inefficiencies cascade into downstream
applications like inference-time scaling, reasoning, and reinforcement
learning, which are inference-bottlenecked, ultimately hindering
scalability \[[3](#bib.bib27)\].

Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as the leading
non-autoregressive alternative for language modeling \[[6](#bib.bib5),
[7](#bib.bib32), [8](#bib.bib12)\], with recent efforts scaling them to
billions of parameters \[[9](#bib.bib19), [10](#bib.bib18),
[11](#bib.bib20), [12](#bib.bib28), [13](#bib.bib29)\]. In contrast to
fixed causal orderings, MDMs model any-order factorizations of the
sequence by training on arbitrary masking patterns. During inference,
this permits adaptive unmask-and-remask decoding strategies that commit
high-confidence tokens first \[[14](#bib.bib48), [15](#bib.bib51),
[16](#bib.bib52)\]. Such a flexible generative procedure has proven
useful in planning-oriented tasks \[[17](#bib.bib41)\].

Complementing discrete formulations, a distinct line of work explores
diffusion and flows within continuous representations for
non-autoregressive language modeling, spanning fixed
embeddings \[[18](#bib.bib6), [19](#bib.bib8), [20](#bib.bib50)\],
learned latent spaces \[[21](#bib.bib7), [22](#bib.bib47)\], and one-hot
relaxations \[[23](#bib.bib9), [24](#bib.bib10), [25](#bib.bib13)\].
Recently, continuous-space approaches have been shown to be competitive
with their discrete-diffusion counterparts in language
modeling \[[26](#bib.bib37), [22](#bib.bib47), [20](#bib.bib50),
[27](#bib.bib53)\]. In particular, Flow Map Language Models
(FMLMs) \[[26](#bib.bib37)\] train flow maps \[[28](#bib.bib1)\] over
one-hot embeddings in Euclidean space, resolving the inherent
factorization error in MDMs \[[29](#bib.bib17), [30](#bib.bib21),
[31](#bib.bib14)\] by learning a joint transport from Gaussian noise to
one-hot vectors. This allows FMLMs to substantially improve the quality
of few-step language generation, including generating text in just a
_single_ function evaluation \[[26](#bib.bib37)\].

Beyond fast, parallel inference, non-autoregressive generation offers a
more profound theoretical advantage over AR modeling: the capacity for
_iterative refinement_ of generated text. While traditional causal
language models are fundamentally constrained by a one-way,
left-to-right generation, an iterative refinement paradigm allows the
model to globally critique, erase, and regenerate arbitrary subsets of
tokens to continually improve its output. This capacity directly mirrors
human cognition; when composing complex text, humans rarely write
perfectly in a single, unyielding left-to-right pass. Instead, we
efficiently formulate a rough draft to capture the global context, and
then iteratively assess, delete, and rewrite specific parts of text
while keeping the overall picture in context \[[32](#bib.bib58)\].

However, existing non-autoregressive paradigms fail to fully realize
this potential. While MDMs offer flexible, any-order inference, their
quality rapidly degrades when multiple tokens are unmasked
simultaneously, rendering few-step generation
infeasible \[[29](#bib.bib17), [30](#bib.bib21), [31](#bib.bib14),
[26](#bib.bib37)\]. On the contrary, FMLMs resolve this factorization
error by learning the joint transport from Gaussian noise to one-hot
vectors, yet they lack the inference-time flexibility native to MDMs
because they evolve all tokens simultaneously. We argue that the
respective strengths of these two paradigms constitute the core
primitives for effective iterative refinement, which requires both —
efficient drafting of coherent multi-token blocks and the flexibility to
retain arbitrary token subsets while regenerating the rest.

Motivated by this insight, we introduce $`\text{FMLM}+`$, a unified
framework that equips FMLMs with masking-style noise schedules. By
coupling single-step sequence generation from FMLMs with flexible
conditioning from MDMs, this architecture naturally supports iterative
refinement. Crucially, because the entire sequence is transported
jointly, our approach yields an _a posteriori_ confidence score for each
token _conditioned on the full draft_. This contrasts sharply with the
_a priori_ confidence derived from independent token-wise marginals in
MDMs. We leverage this property to develop _Posterior Refinement_ (PR) —
an iterative refinement strategy that recursively retains
high-confidence tokens and regenerates the rest to keep improving sample
quality with each additional round of refinement
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In Introduction ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
Subsequently, $`\text{FMLM}+`$ with Posterior Refinement establishes a
new state-of-the-art that consistently outperforms both MDM and FMLM
baselines across all considered benchmarks with far fewer function
evaluations (NFEs).

Our contributions are as follows:

1.  1.  A unifying framework. We introduce $`\text{FMLM}+`$, a
        generalization of FMLMs to masking-style noise schedules that
        combines the few-step efficiency of FMLMs with the any-order
        flexibility of MDMs. We further establish a connection between MDMs
        and $`\text{FMLM}+`$, providing a direct path to scale
        $`\text{FMLM}+`$ leveraging advances in large-scale MDM
        pre-training \[[9](#bib.bib19), [10](#bib.bib18)\].
2.  2.  Posterior refinement. We introduce _Posterior Refinement_, an
        _after-the-fact_ confidence-based strategy that enables
        $`\text{FMLM}+`$ to recursively self-correct its output while
        generating all remaining tokens with single function evaluations
        ([Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In Introduction ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
        We identify how existing a-priori confidence heuristics of MDMs fail
        on simple toy problems and demonstrate how Posterior Refinement is
        able to rectify these shortcomings.
3.  3.  Extensive evaluation. We demonstrate that $`\text{FMLM}+`$ navigates
        the speed–quality trade-off more effectively than both MDM and FMLM
        families across four benchmarks: TinyStories \[[33](#bib.bib40)\],
        OpenWebText \[[34](#bib.bib35)\], GSM8K \[[35](#bib.bib38)\], and
        Sudoku, matching or surpassing the strongest baselines with up to
        $`32\times`$ fewer NFEs.

Figure 2: Posterior Refinement with $`\text{FMLM}+`$. By evaluating
token consistency against the full generated sequence, $`\text{FMLM}+`$
effectively identifies its own errors. Crucially, incorrect tokens
consistently form a subset of low-confidence generations, allowing
Posterior Refinement to reliably filter and revise errors.

## Background

Let $`\mathcal{V}`$ denote a vocabulary, with $`|\mathcal{V}|=V`$, and
let $`{\bf y}=({\bf y}^{l})_{l=1}^{L}\in\mathcal{V}^{L}`$ be a sequence
of length $`L`$ drawn from a data distribution $`p({\bf y})`$.

#### Autoregressive Models.

The AR paradigm models the data distribution through a left-to-right
factorization
$`p({\bf y})=p({\bf y}^{1})p({\bf y}^{2}|{\bf y}^{1})\ldots p({\bf y}^{L}|{\bf y}^{<L})`$,
and learns the conditional distributions
$`p({\bf y}^{l}\mid{\bf y}^{<l})`$ over tokens given their preceding
context \[[36](#bib.bib31), [37](#bib.bib34), [38](#bib.bib30)\].
Generation proceeds sequentially by sampling one token at a time
conditioned on previously generated tokens.

#### Masked Diffusion Models.

Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) \[[6](#bib.bib5), [7](#bib.bib32),
[8](#bib.bib12)\] offer an alternative paradigm for discrete generative
modeling, parameterizing marginals over clean tokens given a partially
masked input. MDMs extend the vocabulary $`\mathcal{V}`$ with an extra
$`[\texttt{MASK}]`$ token. A monotonic fraction $`\alpha(t)`$ of clean
tokens $`{\bf y}`$ is masked to produce $`{\bf y}_{t}`$. The token-wise
marginal $`p_{\theta}({\bf y}^{l}\mid{\bf y}_{t})`$ is then trained via
a classification loss over the masked positions,

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{MDM}}(p_{\theta})=-\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[w(t)\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathbf{1}[{\bf y}_{t}^{l}=\texttt{MASK}]\log p_{\theta}({\bf y}^{l}\mid{\bf y}_{t})\right],`$ |     | (1) |

where $`w(t)>0`$ is some weighting function.

At inference, MDMs start from a fully masked sequence and generate
tokens via an iterative unmask–remask procedure; at each step they first
categorically sample from the marginal distribution for each token
independently and then remask some tokens, repeating until all tokens
are unmasked. A natural decoding strategy for MDMs is to commit tokens
in decreasing order of confidence, usually using the maximum marginal
probability
$`\max_{v}p_{\theta}({\bf y}^{l}=v\mid{\bf y}_{t})`$ \[[15](#bib.bib51),
[16](#bib.bib52)\].

#### Flow Matching and Flow Maps.

Flow matching \[[39](#bib.bib3), [40](#bib.bib33), [41](#bib.bib2)\]
learns a continuous transport from a simple source distribution (e.g.,
Gaussian noise) to the target data distribution by regressing the
velocity field of a probability flow ODE along a prescribed
source–target interpolant. We define $`{\bf x}_{1}=f({\bf y})`$ as the
one-hot representation of clean data, and sample
$`{\bf x}_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I)`$ as isotropic Gaussian noise of
matching shape to construct the linear interpolant in Euclidean space:

|     |                                                                                 |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle I_{t}\coloneqq(1-t){\bf x}_{0}+t{\bf x}_{1},\qquad t\in[0,1].`$ |     | (2) |

This interpolant admits a deterministic probability flow ODE

|     |                                                                                                                                                                            |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\dot{\bf x}_{t}=b_{t}({\bf x}_{t}),\qquad b_{t}({\bf x})=\mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_{t}\mid I_{t}={\bf x}]=\mathbb{E}[{\bf x}_{1}-{\bf x}_{0}\mid I_{t}={\bf x}],`$ |     | (3) |

whose solution transports samples from the source distribution to the
target data distribution \[[39](#bib.bib3), [40](#bib.bib33),
[41](#bib.bib2)\]. In practice, we parameterize the flow velocity
$`b_{t}`$ with a neural network, and inference requires a numerical
integration of the probability flow ODE to generate samples.

The flow map
$`X_{s,t}:[0,1]^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{L\times V}\to\mathbb{R}^{L\times V}`$
associated with the velocity field $`b_{t}`$ is defined as the solution
operator that transports the state at time $`s`$ to the state at time
$`t`$ \[[28](#bib.bib1)\]:

|     |                                                                                                                                     |     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle X_{s,t}({\bf x}_{s})={\bf x}_{s}+\int_{s}^{t}b_{\tau}({\bf x}_{\tau})d\tau={\bf x}_{s}+(t-s)v_{s,t}({\bf x}_{s}),`$ |     | (4) |

where $`v_{s,t}({\bf x}_{s})`$ is the average velocity (mean flow)
between times $`s`$ and $`t`$ \[[42](#bib.bib15)\]. In the limit
$`s\to t`$, the average velocity recovers the instantaneous velocity,
$`\lim_{s\to t}v_{s,t}({\bf x})=b_{t}({\bf x})`$. Crucially, this allows
us to arbitrarily jump along the flow, including generating from the
target distribution in a _single_ function evaluation
($`X_{0,1}`$) \[[43](#bib.bib16), [42](#bib.bib15)\].

#### Flow Map Language Models.

Flow map language models (FMLM) \[[26](#bib.bib37)\] enable few-step
language generation by parameterizing the _two-time denoiser_ (TTD)
$`\delta_{s,t}:[0,1]^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{L\times V}\to\mathbb{R}^{L\times V}`$,

|     |                                        |                                                          |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\delta_{s,t}({\bf x})`$ | $`\displaystyle\coloneqq{\bf x}+(1-s)v_{s,t}({\bf x}),`$ |     | (5) |

which extrapolates the flow-map transport to $`t=1`$ and satisfies the
boundary identity
$`\delta_{t,t}({\bf x})=\mathbb{E}[{\bf x}_{1}\mid I_{t}={\bf x}]`$ \[[44](#bib.bib54),
[45](#bib.bib36), [26](#bib.bib37)\]. The TTD takes values on the
per-token simplex, $`\delta_{s,t}({\bf x})^{l}\in\Delta^{V-1}`$ for
$`l=1,\dots,L`$, and obeys the semigroup identity

|     |                                                                                                                                                             |     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\delta_{s,t}({\bf x})=\gamma\,\delta_{s,u}({\bf x})+(1-\gamma)\,\delta_{u,t}(X_{s,u}({\bf x})),\qquad\gamma=\frac{(1-t)(u-s)}{(1-u)(t-s)},`$ |     | (6) |

for every $`0\leq s\leq u\leq t\leq 1`$ \[[26](#bib.bib37)\]. In
practice, we parameterize $`{\delta}_{s,t}`$ with a token-wise softmax
head and train it via a token-wise cross-entropy objective,

|     |                                                        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{FMLM}}({\delta})`$ | $`\displaystyle\coloneqq\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t}\mathbb{E}_{{\bf x}_{0},{\bf x}_{1}}\left[\text{CE}\left({\delta}_{s,s}(I_{s}),{\bf x}_{1}\right)\right]}_{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diag}}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{s,u,t}\mathbb{E}_{{\bf x}_{0},{\bf x}_{1}}\left[\text{CE}\left({\delta}_{s,t}(I_{s}),\bar{\delta}_{s,t}\right)\right]}_{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{off}}},`$ |     | (7) |

where
$`X_{s,u}({\bf x})\coloneqq\frac{1-u}{1-s}\,{\bf x}+\frac{u-s}{1-s}\,\delta_{s,u}({\bf x})`$,
$`\bar{\delta}_{s,t}\coloneqq\text{stopgrad}\left({\gamma\,\delta_{s,u}(I_{s})+(1-\gamma)\,\delta_{u,t}(X_{s,u}(I_{s}))}\right)`$.
Intuitively, this loss trains the two-time denoiser to reconstruct clean
data along the diagonal $`s=t`$ ($`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diag}}`$) and to
progressively distill a larger off-diagonal jump ($`s\rightarrow t`$)
using two smaller jumps ($`s\rightarrow u,u\rightarrow t`$) as a teacher
($`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{off}}`$).

During inference, we can arbitrarily jump along the flow by recovering
the flow map from the TTD,

|     |                                                                                                     |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle X_{s,t}({\bf x})=\frac{1-t}{1-s}\,{\bf x}+\frac{t-s}{1-s}\,\delta_{s,t}({\bf x}).`$ |     | (8) |

This allows us to generate samples in as few as a _single_ function
evaluation ($`\delta_{0,1}`$).

## FMLM+

Continuous diffusion and flow-based models typically denoise the full
sequence in parallel \[[46](#bib.bib24), [47](#bib.bib4),
[39](#bib.bib3)\]. While effective for unconditional generation, this
formulation has no native mechanism for conditioning on clean context.
Unlike autoregressive or masked models, where conditioning is a
structural primitive, continuous-flow models often require architectural
modifications, such as cross-attention or auxiliary guidance models, to
incorporate conditional information \[[48](#bib.bib43),
[49](#bib.bib44)\]. To address this limitation in flow-based language
modeling, we introduce $`\text{FMLM}+`$, a generalization of FMLMs that
natively learns to generate under diverse conditioning patterns
([Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "Training ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
We show that this allows for flexible decoding strategies at inference
time
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "Inference ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")),
such as FMLM- and MDM- like inference, and further unlocks novel
iterative refinement schemes
([Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "Posterior Refinement ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).

### Training

The key idea underlying $`\text{FMLM}+`$ is to generalize FMLMs by
lifting the noising process to a masking-style design, preserving a set
of clean tokens $`{\bf y}^{\mathcal{C}}`$ at context positions
$`\mathcal{C}\subset\{1,\cdots,L\}`$ while noising the rest:

|                                                                                                      |                                                                                                |     |     |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|                                                                                                      | $`\displaystyle I*{t}^{l}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\mathbf{x}*{1}^{l},&\text{if }l\in\mathcal{C}\\ |
| (1-t)\mathbf{x}_{0}^{l}+t\mathbf{x}_{1}^{l},&\text{else }(l\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}).\end{cases}`$ |                                                                                                | (9) |

This enables $`\text{FMLM}+`$ to condition on arbitrary clean context
without additional architectural components. In practice, this is
implemented by converting the shared time conditioning in the DiT
architecture \[[50](#bib.bib22)\] to a per-position conditioning with
$`t=1`$ for clean positions. For brevity, we drop this implicit
conditioning on $`{\bf y}^{\mathcal{C}}`$ throughout the remainder of
the paper, writing $`\delta_{s,t}(\cdot)`$ instead of
$`\delta_{s,t}(\cdot|{\bf y}^{\mathcal{C}})`$.

We train the two-time denoiser $`\delta_{s,t}`$ with the following
progressive self-distillation objective:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{FMLM}+}(\delta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{C}}\Big[\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t}\,\mathbb{E}_{{\bf x}_{0},{\bf x}_{1}}\!\big[\mathrm{CE}(\delta_{s,s}(I_{s}),{\bf x}_{1})\odot m\big]}_{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diag}}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{s,u,t}\,\mathbb{E}_{{\bf x}_{0},{\bf x}_{1}}\!\big[\mathrm{CE}(\delta_{s,t}(I_{s}),\bar{\delta}_{s,t})\odot m\big]}_{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{off}}}\Big].`$ |     | (10) |

Compared to the vanilla FMLM objective
[Equation 7](#S2.E7 "In Flow Map Language Models. ‣ Background ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps"),
we have an additional expectation over $`\mathcal{C}`$, the set of
context tokens, and use $`m\in\{0,1\}^{L}`$ with
$`m^{l}=\mathbf{1}[\,l\notin\mathcal{C}\,]`$ to mask the loss from
tokens that are already clean. To avoid extra complexity, we drop the
time reparameterization trick from [Lee et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib37) and
use the self-distillation
objective ([10](#S3.E10 "Equation 10 ‣ Training ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps"))
instead of the two-stage training in [Lee et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib37) for
all $`\text{FMLM}+`$ runs.

#### Leveraging Pretrained MDMs.

To accelerate the training of $`\text{FMLM}+`$, we propose a novel
method to leverage pretrained MDMs based on the following observation.
At $`s=t=0`$, the off-diagonal term $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{off}}`$ in
the $`\text{FMLM}+`$ training objective
[Equation 10](#S3.E10 "In Training ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")
vanishes and the diagonal term $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diag}}`$ reduces
to:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                 |     |      |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{C}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{{\bf x}_{0},{\bf x}_{1}}\left[\text{CE}(\delta_{0,0}({\bf x}_{0}),{\bf x}_{1})\odot m\right]\right].`$ |     | (11) |

This token-wise classification objective predicts the ground-truth
tokens using only the context $`{\bf y}^{\mathcal{C}}`$ and pure
Gaussian noise. Because the model must rely exclusively on the context,
this formulation is equivalent to MDM training objective
[Equation 1](#S2.E1 "In Masked Diffusion Models. ‣ Background ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps"),
which similarly predicts targets from $`{\bf y}^{\mathcal{C}}`$ and
$`[\texttt{MASK}]`$ tokens.

We use this equivalence to accelerate $`\text{FMLM}+`$ training in two
ways:

1.  1.  Distillation. We utilize an MDM as a teacher model, training the
        $`\text{FMLM}+`$ student to match the MDM’s token probabilities for
        the same context. This approach reduces gradient variance and
        accelerates convergence \[[51](#bib.bib45)\]. Concretely, we use:

    |     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |     |      |
    | --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
    |     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{Distill}}(\delta)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{\text{FMLM}+}}(\delta)+\lambda\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bf x}_{0},{\bf x}_{1}}\left[\text{CE}(\delta_{0,0}(I_{0}),p_{\theta}({\bf y}_{0}))\right].`$ |     | (12) |

2.  2.  Initialization. We initialize $`\text{FMLM}+`$ weights directly from
        a pretrained MDM checkpoint, leveraging the similarity between the
        masked diffusion and continuous flow
        objectives \[[52](#bib.bib46)\]. We show how the DiT architecture
        can mechanistically adapt MDM weights to handle noisy input
        in [Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "Leveraging Pretrained MDMs ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").

Figure 3: Improved Training Techniques for $`\text{FMLM}+`$. _Left:_
downstream accuracy ($`\uparrow`$) with 32 rounds of Posterior
Refinement; both teacher-based variants outperform training from
scratch. _Right:_ training loss ($`\downarrow`$); warm-started training
converges faster and achieves a better optimum. Both metrics are
smoothened with an exponential moving average ($`\lambda=0.99`$).

Empirically, both distillation and initialization strategies
significantly improve training efficiency and final performance. We find
that warm starting from pre-trained MDM weights helps the model converge
to a better optimum than training from scratch, highlighting the role of
stochasticity and parameter initialization in training FMLMs
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In Leveraging Pretrained MDMs. ‣ Training ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).

### Inference

 

Algorithm 4 $`\text{FMLM}+`$ Inference.

 

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\# delta: Two Time Denoiser

\# C: commit criterion; R rounds

x = randn(L, V)

s, t = zeros(L), ones(L)

for \_ in range(R):

x_1 = delta(x, s, t, flow_steps)

tokens = x_1.argmax(axis=1)

commit = C(tokens, x_1)

x = where(commit,

one_hot(tokens), randn(L, V))

s = where(commit, 1, 0)

return x_1

 

The core advantage of training $`\text{FMLM}+`$ on diverse conditioning
patterns is that it allows us to flexibly choose between various
decoding strategies during inference. As a simple example, we can
recover the standard FMLM inference by defining a time grid
$`0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{N}=1`$ and denoising all unknown tokens
simultaneously, jumping in $`N`$ steps along the flow trajectory
via [Equation 8](#S2.E8 "In Flow Map Language Models. ‣ Background ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").

More importantly, this allows us to construct a mechanism for iterative
refinement as a loop that performs parallel generation followed by
committing a subset of tokens
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "Inference ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
At each iteration $`i`$, we propose a candidate $`\hat{\bf x}_{1}`$ via
FMLM inference. Then, we select a subset $`\mathcal{U}`$ to retain from
this candidate sequence and round them into discrete tokens via an
$`\argmax`$ operation. Finally, we add them to our context set
$`\mathcal{C}\coloneqq\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{U}`$ and re-noise all
remaining tokens $`[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}`$ for the next iteration.
This, for example, allows for block-diffusion-style
inference \[[53](#bib.bib56)\] by choosing $`\mathcal{U}`$ as the next
contiguous block of $`B`$ tokens.

We may further perform MDM-like, confidence-based inference by noting
the equivalence between $`\delta_{0,0}`$ and MDMs
([11](#S3.E11 "Equation 11 ‣ Leveraging Pretrained MDMs. ‣ Training ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
Consequently, by sampling tokens from $`\delta_{0,0}({\bf x}_{0})`$ and
by prioritizing positions with sharper $`\delta_{0,0}({\bf x}_{0})`$, we
recover MDM’s confidence-based sampling \[[15](#bib.bib51),
[16](#bib.bib52), [17](#bib.bib41)\]. We note that this approach,
applied either to $`\text{FMLM}+`$ with $`\delta_{0,0}`$ or MDMs,
generates tokens and estimates confidence _a priori_, using only the
partial context available at that step and without knowing what tokens
will be generated at other positions.

### Posterior Refinement

Beyond recovering existing inference schemes as in
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "Inference ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps"),
we show that $`\text{FMLM}+`$ enables a novel class of after-the-fact
refinement strategies native to neither the MDM nor the FMLM paradigms.

During inference, $`\text{FMLM}+`$ steps along the flow trajectory to
simultaneously decode all positions. At the final integration step,
because the model operates on a nearly complete sequence, the model
implicitly evaluates the conditional probability of each token given the
rest of the generated text. The one-step generation $`\delta_{0,1}`$
also captures this behavior since, ideally, the flow from $`t=0`$ to
$`t=1`$ is equivalent to composing the transport from $`0`$ to $`t`$ and
the flow map jump from $`t`$ to $`1`$. This enables us to compute token
confidence conditioned on the fully generated sequence, effectively
evaluating each token’s fit within the global context. Reflecting the
_a-posteriori_ nature of these estimates, we term our approach
_Posterior Refinement_ (PR).

PR instantiates the inference loop in
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "Inference ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps"),
choosing the retained set $`\mathcal{U}`$ using the confidence of the
predicted endpoint. Concretely, at each iteration, we use the final flow
map jump $`\hat{\bf x}_{1}=\delta_{t_{N-1},1}({\bf x}_{t_{N-1}})`$ to
set

|     |                                                                                    |     |      |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{U}=\{l\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}:p_{\text{max}}^{l}>p\},`$ |     | (13) |

where
$`p_{\text{max}}^{l}\coloneqq\max_{v}(\hat{\bf x}_{1}^{(i)})^{l,v}`$ is
a measure of the a-posteriori confidence and $`p`$ is some threshold for
selecting confident tokens. To avoid stalling when no position clears
the threshold, we commit at least $`k`$ positions per round, falling
back to the top-$`k`$ by confidence.

#### Interpretation.

![Refer to caption](2606.24773v1/a_priori_vs_a_posteriori_two_mode.png)

Figure 5: Two types of confidence. On a 2-mode toy problem, the one-step
FMLM $`\delta_{0,1}`$ outputs high $`p_{\max}`$ for most inputs.
Low-confidence regions concentrate near decision boundaries, where the
endpoint is ambiguous, indicating $`\delta_{0,1}`$ captures the
epistemic confidence of the model. In contrast, $`\delta_{0,0}`$ is flat
for all inputs, reflecting its aleatoric nature.

An ideal FMLM would perfectly sample from its training distribution,
always producing one-hot vectors. In practice, however, the model
outputs categorical distributions that are not strictly one-hot. To
resolve this, [Lee et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib37) project each token to the
nearest vertex of the probability simplex via the argmax operator. We
interpret the _rounding error_ of this projection as a proxy for the
model’s confidence. This interpretation aligns with our empirical
observations in Sudoku, where we find that incorrect tokens consistently
exhibit high rounding error
([Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In Introduction ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).

Concretely, this rounding error can be quantified using either the
$`\ell_{1}`$ distance or the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between
the generated distribution and the target one-hot distribution. Under
both metrics, the rounding error is a monotonically decreasing function
of $`p_{\max}^{l}`$. Consequently, applying a threshold to
$`p_{\max}^{l}`$ is mathematically equivalent to thresholding the
rounding error under these metrics
([Proposition A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition A.1 (Rounding error is monotone in confidence). ‣ Rounding error in terms of confidence ‣ Appendix A Theoretical details ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).

#### Why a-priori confidence fails.

Because both the MDM denoiser $`p_{\theta}`$ and the FMLM denoiser
$`\delta_{0,0}`$ predict token-wise marginals, independently sampling
high-confidence tokens from these marginals cannot circumvent
factorization error. While this heuristic performs well on unimodal
target distributions such as unique Sudoku solutions, it
catastrophically fails on multi-modal distributions
([Table 6](#S4.T6 "In Posterior Refinement ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
We identify that MDMs, and equivalently $`\delta_{0,0}`$, conflate
aleatoric uncertainty, the inherent randomness of the data distribution,
with epistemic uncertainty, the model’s internal
confidence \[[54](#bib.bib55)\]. We hypothesize that by failing to
perfectly learn the joint transport from Gaussian noise to clean one-hot
data, the FMLM trajectory is able to surface the true epistemic
uncertainty of the model through errors in its predictions
([Figure 5](#S3.F5 "In Interpretation. ‣ Posterior Refinement ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).

## Experiments

We evaluate $`\text{FMLM}+`$ on four benchmarks:
TinyStories \[[33](#bib.bib40)\] and OpenWebText \[[34](#bib.bib35)\]
for unconditional language generation, TinyGSM \[[55](#bib.bib39)\] for
conditional reasoning, and Sudoku for structured constraint
satisfaction. Following [Kim et al. \[17\]](#bib.bib41), we train on
code solutions from the synthetic TinyGSM corpus and evaluate zero-shot
on the GSM8K \[[35](#bib.bib38)\] test split. We adopt a
DiT \[[50](#bib.bib22)\] backbone for all baselines; further details on
model architecture and datasets are provided
in [Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Setup ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").

#### Training.

We train $`\text{FMLM}+`$ with AdamW under bfloat16 mixed precision,
optimizing the Two-Time Denoiser self-distillation objective
in [Equation 10](#S3.E10 "In Training ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").
For the MDM-distillation and -initialization experiments
([Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "Leveraging Pretrained MDMs ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")),
we additionally train an MDLM model \[[8](#bib.bib12)\] with the same
architecture to act as a teacher and an initialization checkpoint
respectively.
[Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "limit-from"FMLM"+ training objective ‣ Appendix B Setup ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")
specifies all task-specific training hyperparameters.

#### Evaluation.

On TinyStories and OpenWebText, we report generative perplexity under
GPT-2 Large \[[56](#bib.bib23)\] together with per-sample unigram
entropy; where low entropy signals repetition
collapse \[[30](#bib.bib21)\]. We report solve-rate accuracy using a
sampled Python solution graded by execution for GSM8K and a valid
completion respecting the clue set for Sudoku.

Figure 9: adaLN activations. At $`t{=}0`$, noisy inputs align with the
MDM’s $`[\texttt{MASK}]`$ activation while remaining uncorrelated with
other tokens.

The strong performance of $`\text{FMLM}+`$ (Init) in
[Table 8](#S4.T8 "In Leveraging Pretrained MDMs ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")
is surprising, since it is unclear why pretraining on
$`[\texttt{MASK}]`$ tokens should benefit processing Gaussian-noise
inputs. We explain this by inspecting two components of the DiT
backbone, the first adaptive layer normalization
(adaLN) \[[57](#bib.bib42)\] for time conditioning, and the token
embedding layer, before and after $`\text{FMLM}+`$ training. For the
first DiT block, we measure the cosine similarity between
$`\text{FMLM}+`$’s post-adaLN activations and those of the MDM teacher’s
([Figure 9](#S4.F9 "In Leveraging Pretrained MDMs ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
At $`t{=}0`$ (pure Gaussian noise), $`\text{FMLM}+`$ activations remain
highly aligned with the teacher’s $`[\texttt{MASK}]`$ activations. Thus,
we conclude that the first adaLN layer maps the Gaussian-noise input
onto the same representation the teacher produced for
$`[\texttt{MASK}]`$ tokens, presenting downstream layers with an
in-distribution input and preserving the pretrained knowledge. In
[Table 12](#A3.T12 "In Leveraging Pretrained MDMs ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps"),
we further compute the per-token cosine similarity between each
$`\text{FMLM}+`$ input embedding and its MDM-init counterpart. Every
token embedding stays aligned with its initialization after training,
indicating that $`\text{FMLM}+`$ adapts the embedding layer to be robust
to Gaussian noise corruptions.

## Conclusion

We introduce $`\text{FMLM}+`$, a generalization of flow map language
models that equips continuous-flow language modeling with the any-order
inference flexibility of masked diffusion, paving the way towards
effective iterative refinement. We further introduce _Posterior
Refinement_, a novel, after-the-fact refinement strategy that re-noises
and regenerates low-confidence tokens to self-correct in parallel.
Empirically, $`\text{FMLM}+`$ improves the speed-quality tradeoff over
both MDM and FMLM families across unconditional and conditional
generation settings, matching or surpassing the strongest baselines with
up to $`32{\times}`$ fewer function evaluations. Finally, we show that
the masked diffusion objective is equivalent to a boundary case of the
$`\text{FMLM}+`$ training objective, and use this correspondence to
derive two practical mechanisms based on distillation and transfer
learning for accelerating $`\text{FMLM}+`$ training using pretrained
MDMs.

#### Future directions.

The correspondence between MDM and $`\text{FMLM}+`$ offers a path to
scale $`\text{FMLM}+`$ to the billion-parameter regime using the growing
pool of large pretrained masked diffusion models (LLaDA-8B
\[[9](#bib.bib19)\], Dream \[[10](#bib.bib18)\], and others). We also
believe that the conditional nature of $`\text{FMLM}+`$ can be leveraged
to improve generation quality using techniques such as classifier-free
guidance \[[58](#bib.bib59)\]. Finally, Posterior Refinement exposes a
form of inference-time scaling native to $`\text{FMLM}+`$, and we expect
novel test-time strategies can be designed around such
posterior-confidence signals. We leave a systematic study of these
directions to future work.

#### Limitations.

Methodologically, we follow the progressive self-distillation objective
from [Lee et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib37) and do not explore alternatives
such as the Lagrangian, Eulerian and Mean Flow
variants \[[28](#bib.bib1), [42](#bib.bib15)\]. We conduct our
experiments on a small scale on largely synthetic and small-sized
datasets. Thus, the scalability of our approach needs a more broad study
with evaluation on downstream tasks. While our current formulation of PR
holds committed tokens fixed, alternative formulations can be explored
to allow $`\text{FMLM}+`$ to rectify previous errors. Finally, we note
that training from scratch is suboptimal compared to initializing with
MDM weights, even at convergence. This implies that there is room to
improve $`\text{FMLM}+`$ training with better model architecture and
low-variance loss functions.

## Appendix A Theoretical details

### Rounding error in terms of confidence

In
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "Interpretation. ‣ Posterior Refinement ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")
we interpret the _rounding error_ that occurs when model prediction is
projected to its nearest one-hot vertex as a proxy for the model’s
confidence. We claim that thresholding this error is equivalent to
thresholding the top probability $`p_{\max}^{l}`$ and show it here.

Fix a position $`l`$ and write $`q\coloneqq Q^{l}\in\Delta^{|V|-1}`$ for
the predicted categorical distribution, with top probability
$`p_{\max}\coloneqq\max_{v}q^{v}`$ attained at
$`\hat{v}\coloneqq\argmax_{v}q^{v}`$. Committing the token rounds $`q`$
to the one-hot vertex $`e_{\hat{v}}`$, and the rounding error is the
discrepancy between $`q`$ and $`e_{\hat{v}}`$, measured either by the
$`\ell_{1}`$ distance or by the KL divergence.

###### Proposition A.1 (Rounding error is monotone in confidence).

With the notation above,

|     |                                                                                                                        |     |      |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bigl\|q-e_{\hat{v}}\bigr\|_{1}=2\,(1-p_{\max}),\qquad\mathsf{KL}(e_{\hat{v}}\>\|\>q)=-\log p_{\max}.`$ |     | (14) |

Both quantities are strictly decreasing in $`p_{\max}\in(0,1]`$,
vanishing exactly at $`p_{\max}=1`$. Consequently, for any threshold
$`p\in(0,1]`$,

|     |                                                                                                                                       |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle p_{\max}\geq p\;\iff\;\bigl\|q-e_{\hat{v}}\bigr\|_{1}\leq 2(1-p)\;\iff\;\mathsf{KL}(e_{\hat{v}}\>\|\>q)\leq-\log p,`$ |     | (15) |

so thresholding the confidence $`p_{\max}`$ and thresholding the
rounding error under either metric retain exactly the same set of
positions.

###### Proof.

The mass that $`q`$ places off the top token is
$`\sum_{v\neq\hat{v}}q^{v}=1-p_{\max}`$. For the $`\ell_{1}`$ distance,

|     |                                                      |                    |                            |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bigl\|q-e*{\hat{v}}\bigr\|*{1}=\bigl | q^{\hat{v}}-1\bigr | +\sum\_{v\neq\hat{v}}\bigl | q^{v}\bigr | =(1-p*{\max})+\sum*{v\neq\hat{v}}q^{v}=2\,(1-p\_{\max}).`$ |     | (16) |

For the KL divergence, only the $`v=\hat{v}`$ term survives, since
$`e_{\hat{v}}^{v}=0`$ for $`v\neq\hat{v}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                           |     |      |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(e_{\hat{v}}\>\|\>q)=\sum_{v}e_{\hat{v}}^{v}\log\frac{e_{\hat{v}}^{v}}{q^{v}}=1\cdot\log\frac{1}{q^{\hat{v}}}=-\log p_{\max}.`$ |     | (17) |

Both $`2(1-p_{\max})`$ and $`-\log p_{\max}`$ are continuous and
strictly decreasing on $`(0,1]`$, so each is invertible; applying the
inverse to either rounding-error threshold recovers the confidence
threshold, giving the equivalences in
[Equation 15](#A1.E15 "In Proposition A.1 (Rounding error is monotone in confidence). ‣ Rounding error in terms of confidence ‣ Appendix A Theoretical details ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").
∎

## Appendix B Setup

We document the configurations used to produce all reported results
(summarized in
[Table 11](#A2.T11 "In Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Setup ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps")).
Following prior work \[[8](#bib.bib12), [26](#bib.bib37)\], we adopt a
DiT \[[50](#bib.bib22)\] backbone for $`\text{FMLM}+`$. All experiments
are run on $`4{\times}`$ NVIDIA H100 GPUs, in bfloat16 mixed precision,
with AdamW ($`\beta_{1}{=}0.9`$, $`\beta_{2}{=}0.999`$,
$`\epsilon{=}10^{-8}`$), no weight decay, and gradient-norm clipping at
$`1.0`$. Learning rates follow a $`2.5\text{k}`$-step linear warmup to a
constant peak. We evaluate using exponential moving average (EMA, decay
$`0.9999`$) parameters.

### Datasets

#### TinyStories (unconditional generation).

We train on TinyStories \[[33](#bib.bib40)\], a corpus of
GPT-3.5/4-generated short stories restricted to a limited vocabulary. We
tokenize with the GPT-2 byte-pair tokenizer and pack examples into
length-$`128`$ sequences with \<EOS\>-insertion at sequence boundaries.
We report generative perplexity under GPT-2 Large
following \[[8](#bib.bib12), [29](#bib.bib17), [26](#bib.bib37)\],
alongside per-sample token entropy as a check against entropy collapse.
Results appear in
[Table 7](#S4.T7 "In Posterior Refinement ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").

#### OpenWebText (unconditional generation).

We also evaluate on OpenWebText \[[34](#bib.bib35)\], an open
reproduction of the WebText corpus used to train GPT-2. We tokenize with
the GPT-2 byte-pair tokenizer and pack documents into length-$`1024`$
sequences with \<EOS\>-insertion at document boundaries. As with
TinyStories, we report generative perplexity under GPT-2
Large \[[8](#bib.bib12), [29](#bib.bib17), [26](#bib.bib37)\], alongside
per-sample token entropy as a check against entropy collapse. Results
appear in
[Table 7](#S4.T7 "In Posterior Refinement ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").

#### TinyGSM / GSM8K (conditional reasoning).

We follow the exact protocol of S-FLM \[[59](#bib.bib49)\] so that our
numbers are directly comparable to its baseline suite (MDLM, Duo, CANDI,
FLM, S-FLM). We train on TinyGSM \[[55](#bib.bib39)\], a synthetic
corpus of 12.3M grade-school math word problems generated to imitate the
GSM8K distribution. We tokenize with the SmolLM-135M tokenizer and pack
each $`\langle\text{question},\text{Python solution}\rangle`$ pair to
length $`512`$, with loss supervised only on the solution tokens. Models
are evaluated zero-shot on the GSM8K test split by sampling a Python
solution conditioned on the prompt and grading by execution accuracy.

#### Sudoku (conditional).

Following S-FLM \[[59](#bib.bib49)\], each puzzle is encoded as a
length-$`180`$ sequence over a $`12`$-token vocabulary, with loss
supervised only on the solution positions. Models are evaluated on the
rate at which they produce a valid completion of the clue set across
Easy/Medium/Hard splits. Results appear in
[Table 7](#S4.T7 "In Posterior Refinement ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").

### Architecture

All models use the Diffusion Transformer (DiT)
backbone \[[50](#bib.bib22)\] with adaLN time conditioning. Following
[Lee et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib37), $`\text{FMLM}+`$ uses a _double_ time
embedding ($`s`$ and $`t`$ are both injected through adaLN) so the same
transformer can serve as the two-time denoiser at training and as a
single-time denoiser at $`s{=}t`$. The MDM baselines and the MDM
teachers used for distillation/initialization use the standard
single-time DiT. The exact per-task configurations are listed in
[Table 11](#A2.T11 "In Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Setup ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps");
for the warm-start and distillation variants, $`\text{FMLM}+`$ reuses
the architecture of the corresponding MDM so that initialization is a
parameter-identity copy.

### $`\text{FMLM}+`$ training objective

 

Algorithm 10 $`\text{FMLM}+`$ Training.

 

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

mask = random_mask(y.shape)

\# clean context pinned to t = 1

s, u, t = where(mask, sample_times(), 1.0)

x_1 = one_hot(y)

x_s = (1- s) \* randn(L, V) + s \* x_1

\# self distillation target

d_su = delta(x_s, s, u)

X_su = flowmap(x_s, d_su, s, u)

d_ut = delta(X_su, u, t)

target = lerp(d_su, d_ut, gamma(s, u, t))

diag = CE(delta(x_s, s, s), x_1)

offdiag = CE(delta(x_s, s, t), sg(target))

\# supervise noised positions only

loss = (diag + offdiag) \* mask

 

We train $`\text{FMLM}+`$ with the progressive self-distillation (PSD)
objective in
[Equation 10](#S3.E10 "In Training ‣ FMLM+ ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps"),
instantiated as
[Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "limit-from"FMLM"+ training objective ‣ Appendix B Setup ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").
We fix the following across all datasets:

- •
  Corruption schedule: Noisy positions share a single sampled time
  $`t\!\sim\!\mathcal{U}[0,1]`$, while the rest are pinned to $`t{=}1`$
  as clean context.
- •
  Progressive self-distillation (PSD): the off-diagonal target uses the
  PSD construction of [Lee et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib37) with stop-gradient
  on the teacher branch.
- •
  Time Reparameterization: we drop the time-reparameterization trick
  from [Lee et al. \[26\]](#bib.bib37), and follow a simple
  linear-schedule.
- •
  Diagonal fraction: with probability $`0.5`$ a step uses the diagonal
  cross-entropy term ($`s{=}t`$); otherwise the off-diagonal semigroup
  term. Both supervise only the noisy tokens.
- •
  Antithetic sampling: each minibatch pairs $`(s,u,t)`$ with
  $`(1{-}t,1{-}u,1{-}s)`$ to reduce variance along the time axis.

#### MDM warm-start and distillation.

For the _FMLM+ (Init)_ variant we initialize $`\text{FMLM}+`$ weights
from a same-architecture MDM checkpoint trained on the same dataset. The
initialization is a parameter-identity copy: the only architectural
difference is that $`\text{FMLM}+`$ activates its second time embedding
(initialized to zero so the network behaves identically at step zero).
For the _FMLM+ (Distill)_ variant we additionally hold a frozen MDM
teacher and replace the diagonal target with the teacher’s posterior
with probability $`p_{\mathrm{distill}}`$. The MDM teachers are trained
from scratch with the standard MDLM loss \[[8](#bib.bib12)\] on the same
data, optimizer, and architecture used by the corresponding
$`\text{FMLM}+`$ run.

## Appendix D Ablations

#### Commit threshold.

We sweep the commit threshold $`p\in\{0.9,0.99,0.999\}`$ for Posterior
Refinement on Sudoku-Hard and GSM8K across NFE budgets. On GSM8K,
$`p{=}0.9`$ saturates by 16 NFEs at 8.6%, while $`p{=}0.999`$ continues
improving through 64 NFEs, reaching 19.1%. Similarly, on Sudoku-Hard,
$`p{=}0.999`$ is a better threshold from 4 NFEs onward, reaching 81.4%
at 16 NFEs. We use $`p{=}0.999`$ for the headline results
in [Table 7](#S4.T7 "In Posterior Refinement ‣ Experiments ‣ Posterior Refinement:Fast Language Generation via Any-Order Flow Maps").

$`\text{FMLM}+`$ (PR = 0.9) 4.1 21.2 20.2 19.9 20.9 0 1.6 4.6 6.5 7.8
9.0 8.5 $`\text{FMLM}+`$ (PR = 0.99) 4.1 35.6 51.9 54.6 56.3 0 0.6 5.7
9.7 14.5 16.6 15.0 $`\text{FMLM}+`$ (PR = 0.999) 4.1 26.0 71.2 78.1 81.4

#### Design choices.

We ablate hyperparams of PR sampling on GSM8K (32 NFEs, $`p{=}0.999`$).
We find that resampling renoised cells from fresh noise is important.
Re-using the same initial noise can cause the model to converge to the
same (rejected) predictions, affecting accuracy. We also note that
setting both threshold and Top-K help improve the performance.

|                    |          |
| ------------------ | -------- |
| Configuration      | Acc. (%) |
| Renoising          |          |
| Same Initial Noise | 14.4     |
| New Initial Noise  | 19.0     |
| Commit schedule    |          |
| Threshold          | 12.8     |
| Top-K              | 7.8      |
| Threshold + Top-K  | 19.0     |
| Top-K Value        |          |
| Top-1              | 17.8     |
| Top-2              | 17.8     |
| Top-4              | 16.1     |
| Top-8              | 11.4     |
| Top-K              | 19.0     |

Table 15: Posterior Refinement design ablations. GSM8K accuracy (%,
$`\uparrow`$) at 32 NFEs, $`p{=}0.999`$. Top-K is dynamically set to
follow a linear schedule in the remaining number of tokens and budget.
